subject: SLO mapping and queue-behavior playbook for reserved pools (QuantFrame)
messages:
From: Jessica Simon <ops@quantframe.com>
To: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 14 May 2026 08:03:00 -0700
Subject: Clarify reserved-pool queueing + throughput guarantees

Hi David —

Thanks again for the demo last week. As we move toward a Dedicated purchase, our infra team needs clarity on how Redwood maps SLA commitments to runtime behavior for reserved GPU pools. A few specific asks: 

- If we commit N reserved GPUs, what steady-state throughput (reqs/sec and token/sec) should we expect per pool at typical request sizes (avg prompt 120 tokens, response 60 tokens)?
- When demand spikes beyond reserved capacity, what queueing behavior kicks in? Do requests queue, fail fast, or spill to burst capacity (if configured)?
- How do you define the SLI/SLO boundary for tail-latency vs. throughput? We need a one-page runbook that maps monitored metrics to customer-visible SLO states (green/amber/red) and automated fallbacks.
- Also: we require explicit fallback behavior for preemption windows and a sample contract amendment clause showing credits or mitigation steps.

Can you share a short playbook and the mapping table so our procurement and legal teams can review? Would prefer to have it by EOD PT tomorrow to keep our internal review on track.

Thanks,
Jessica Simon
Sr. Cloud Ops, QuantFrame
[Attachment: quantframe-initial-usage.xlsx (XLSX, 78 KB)]

From: David Kim <david.kim@redwood.com>

Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>, Diego Fernandez <diego.fernandez@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Clarify reserved-pool queueing + throughput guarantees

Hi Jessica —

Appreciate the clear asks. I've put together a short playbook and an SLI->SLO mapping that address your bullets; attaching a draft PDF and a small sample metrics CSV we collected from a workload comparable to what you described. High level answers up-front: 

- Reserved capacity: our customer-visible throughput guarantee is expressed as a pool-level sustained token/sec target (we translate to requests/sec for common prompt/response sizes). For the profile you gave (120/60), a single V100-class reserved GPU is sized for ~18–22 reqs/sec steady state. We include a conservative headroom buffer of ~15% in the documented guarantee.
- Spikes beyond reservation: default behavior is queuing in a short, latency-prioritized window (30–120s configurable). If you enable burst capacity in the contract, requests will spill to burst nodes until the configured burst budget is exhausted; otherwise requests may return 429s once queue depth exceeds configured threshold.
- SLI mapping: we define availability SLO on 95th/99th percentile tail-latency per-route, plus throughput SLO measured as tokens per minute sustained over 5m windows. Attached playbook maps green/amber/red thresholds and automated actions (e.g., scale to burst, apply rate-limits, route to a cheaper model variant).

Next steps: Lauren — can we confirm whether QuantFrame wants burst enabled in the first 90 days? Diego, can you review the SLI thresholds and adjust the queueing windows to what we run in Dedicated?

I attached: slo-draft-quantframe.pdf (draft playbook) and throughput-metrics.csv (sample).

Best,
David Kim
Head of Solutions — Redwood Inference

--

From: Diego Fernandez <diego.fernandez@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Clarify reserved-pool queueing + throughput guarantees

David/Jessica —

Quick tech notes on the draft playbook (quoted below where useful). I validated the sample numbers against our latest Dedicated runtime (A100-like profile):

- Sizing: for the 120/60 token profile, on A100-class hardware we see ~30 reqs/sec per GPU at 16-bit quantization with continuous batching (95th percentile). We recommend we document the guarantee as 25 reqs/sec per GPU (rounded, includes 15% headroom).
- Queueing windows: we run prefix-aware KV caching that reduces effective token work for repeated prompts; however, for cold prefixes queueing is inevitable. Our recommended default queue window is 60s (we set 30s aggressive, 120s tolerant). When queue depth > 5x nominal concurrency, we trigger immediate fallback to burst or model-variant routing.
- Burst routing: burst capacity is implemented as a separate tenant pool with a different cost matrix; it is not preemptible for dedicated-reserved requests until burst budget is exhausted. If legal wants an explicit credit structure, suggest the following clause: "If Redwood is unable to meet the committed throughput due to capacity-related incidents and burst capacity cannot be allocated, customer is eligible for a throughput credit equal to X% of monthly committed fees for the impacted interval (to be defined in the SLO table)."

Attached CSV includes sample p95/p99 latency and tokens/sec curves for three load traces we used. I also added a small table in the playbook proposing the amber state triggers and automated mitigation scripts we can run from the console.

- Diego
Staff Software Engineer, Serving Runtime
